title: Switching to piano, Earl Hines, and returning to New Orleans in 1934
summary: Banjos fell out of favor in the Depression, so he went back to piano in a band built around him, inspired by Earl Hines, then returned to New Orleans in 1934 and played odd jobs.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Because when, after I left that part of the country up there, and I came down there, it was around, getting around in the Depression time, and the people were putting the banjoes down for the ghettos. And I wasn't able to buy a ghetto, so I went back on the piano. And while I was before, while I was up around Monroe, there was some fine banjo players up there I met. And so after these, these majestic ramblers broke up, so Ben Boyden, saxophone player, said, let's you and I organize a band. I said, man, I want you on piano, because you've been around Hot Spring and you done caught on a lot of styles and playing different. I said, you just kind of playing the kind of style of piano I want. I said, well I'll tell you how I learned. I said, I had been listening around there, listening to Earl Hines play a lot, and I said, I got a lot of his record, and I like his style. I said, I stand up there and watched him poison him. I said, and he's so far ahead of his time. I said, I'd like to pick up a style like that. He said, well we go ahead and organize a band and we're going to build it around you. And you just play out and we just play harmony and we build a band around you. So we done that. And I stayed around about four years, just playing the piano with the band, you know. And I was the feature man in the band. So, well, around about 32, 33, 34, things began to get tough out there. The Depression was hitting around that part of the country. It hadn't been there before. And I said, well, I got me a few dollars. I said, I had got married about two years before that. I said, I think I'm going to go back to New Orleans. I said, because, I said, since I'm married, I said, I have a wife. I got something to look out to. And I said, my mother and them, they got a big home now and then. And if I could happen to fall through, I say, I got to take care of this good. So, we left, packed up, left in 1934. And I came back to New Orleans. And I stayed around here a pretty long while. I didn't have nothing to do. And then the WPA opened up. I couldn't get on or nothing. So finally in 19, around about, oh I used to play a little job. I played with George Lewis. I played with different guys. They'd hire me for what I did. I played with Andy, Kid Howard, around in the 30s. When they get a job, they play the banjo and the avatar. When they have the piano, I play the piano. I played at the voice camp back there. There was the players back there, Willie Unfrey was band leader back there. There was the cabaret back there on Basin Street back up there.
